baseline.environment_config: 0.75 CPU / 384 MiB x 3 API + nginx; PostgreSQL 2 CPU / 1024 MiB, max_connections 100; Redis 256 MB allkeys-lru; pool 10+10 per instance
baseline.saturation_point: plateau 10 VU / 161.82 req/s (Scenario C); usable ceiling by scenario: A 100, B 50, C 10 VU
baseline.error_rate: 0.42 % worst on the ladder (Scenario C @ 200 VU)
baseline.primary_bottleneck: SQLAlchemy connection pool wait on the API tier (up to 1758.45 ms of p95)

takeaways.env.conclusion: The engine is allocated 12 CPUs and 3.75 GB in total. PostgreSQL deliberately gets the largest share, so that the component the architecture expects to saturate is the scarce one by design rather than by accident. k6 runs natively on the host and is never containerised, which is how clause 2.2's isolation requirement is met: the system under test has a fixed share of the machine and the generator cannot consume any of it.
takeaways.calib.conclusion_ok: **5.8x headroom.** k6 plus the loopback plus nginx sustain 7941.78 req/s against a static response, while the application tier tops out at 1368.5 req/s doing no work at all. Every throughput figure below is therefore a property of the system, not of the measuring instrument - and it also means Lab 3's 98-222 req/s scale-out curve was measuring its own probe.
takeaways.ladder.chart_conclusion: All three curves are flat from the very first rung, while the dashed line shows what linear scaling would have looked like. The distance between them is the capacity that does not exist. Scenario A serves roughly three times what Scenario C does, which is the cache doing its work: A's reads are answered from Redis, C's end-to-end workflow has to write.
takeaways.ladder.latency_chart_conclusion: The axis is logarithmic because p50 and p99 differ by one to two orders of magnitude at saturation; on a linear axis the median would be a flat line on the baseline and the whole point - that it stayed usable while the tail did not - would be invisible. The three lines fan apart as load rises, which is the visual form of the question clause 2.4 asks. A request's latency is its own service time plus the time it spent queued behind others. Below saturation the queue is usually empty, so both are small. Past it, arrivals and service times vary, so queue length becomes heavy-tailed: a request arriving during a momentary burst waits behind everything already there. The mean is dominated by the many requests that found a short queue; p99 is the few that found a long one, and that population grows super-linearly with utilisation. This is why an average is not a performance specification.
takeaways.sat.conclusion: Read the first two columns together. Throughput plateaus at the very bottom of the ladder in all three scenarios, which says the limiting resource is already fully busy at 10 virtual users - so every one of the 190 extra users at the top of the ladder is waiting rather than working. Yet nothing fails, and p95 stays inside half a second well past the plateau. That is the normal condition of a healthy saturated system, and it is exactly why a throughput figure on its own is not a capacity statement.
takeaways.sat.chart_conclusion: Two stacked panels rather than one frame with two y-axes: requests per second and per cent are unrelated units, and overlaying them would invite a comparison that means nothing. The top panel flattens immediately; the bottom one stays on zero for A and only lifts for C. A system can be fully saturated and still error-free, and these two panels are what separates the two conditions.
takeaways.res.conclusion: **The API tier is the limit, not the database.** Every instance runs at 89.8 % of its own CPU allowance at the top of the ladder while PostgreSQL never passes 29.3 % of its. That inverts what `docs/bottlenecks.md` #3 expected - *database CPU saturates before any application instance does* - and the reason is Lab 4: the cache took the join off the hot path, so what remains is request parsing, validation and JSON serialisation, which is CPU spent in Python on the API tier. Fixing the predicted bottleneck moved the bottleneck somewhere else, which is the normal outcome of fixing one and the reason a baseline is re-measured rather than inherited. It also explains the scale-out result below: three instances help because they add the resource that is actually scarce.
takeaways.scale.conclusion: Three instances give roughly 2.42x the throughput of one, not 3x, and the shortfall is the shared resource: the host's CPU first and PostgreSQL second, since each instance keeps its own pool and three of them open three times the connections to one database. Note also what one instance does across the ladder - its throughput barely moves while its p99 grows without limit, because it is pinned at its own 0.75 CPU ceiling no matter how many users arrive. Lab 3 measured the same scale-out with an entirely different instrument and landed on 71 % efficiency at three instances; a structural property reproduced by two unrelated tools is worth more than either measurement alone.
takeaways.scale.chart_conclusion: The left panel is the raw gain, the right one is what it cost. Efficiency never reaches 100 %, and it does not fall off a cliff either - which is the signature of contention for a shared resource rather than of a hard ceiling.
takeaways.cache.db_conclusion: **98.1 % fewer rows read from PostgreSQL per request, for 2.92x the throughput.** What remains is the uncached catalogue read that Scenario A keeps in its mix on purpose: a scenario that cached to zero would report an infinite speed-up and measure nothing.
takeaways.cache.chart_conclusion: Two panels, two units, no shared axis. The left panel is what the user feels; the right is what the database pays. They move together here, which is the case for a cache - but they are different measurements, and a report that showed only the left one would not have answered clause 2.6.
takeaways.pool.conclusion: The unpooled path stays flat from 33.19 to 88.24 ms across the whole ladder while the pooled one climbs to 1472.69 ms - so **1384.45 ms of p95 is the wait for a connection, before any work begins**. Starving the pool to 2+0 moves the same curve earlier and higher, which is what makes this a demonstration of the mechanism rather than a correlation. At saturation the instances logged the predicted exception verbatim: `QueuePool limit of size 10 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out, timeout 10.00`. `max_connections` was never approached - 31 connections against a ceiling of 100 - so the wall is the per-instance pool, not the server.
takeaways.pool.chart_conclusion: The blue line is a request that never touches the pool and the orange one is the same request plus a single pooled `SELECT 1`. Everything between them is queueing for a connection. The shaded area opening up as load rises *is* the bottleneck, drawn rather than argued.
takeaways.open.conclusion: **p99 is 45.95x worse under the open model for the same offered load.** Note *offered*, not achieved: the two runs did not deliver the same throughput, and that is the finding rather than a flaw in the comparison. Asked for 563 req/s the system delivered 289.23 - 49 % short - with 1412 errors, where the closed model reported 536.87 req/s and zero.
takeaways.open.chart_conclusion: The p50 bars are almost equal and the p99 bars are not remotely so. That is the signature of coordinated omission: the median is barely affected, because most requests are issued while the system is healthy under either model, while the requests the closed model failed to send were precisely the ones that would have been slowest. The damage is concentrated in exactly the number most likely to be quoted in an SLO.
takeaways.tl.chart_conclusion: Each time the top panel steps up, the middle one does not: throughput is already at its ceiling. The bottom panel steps up instead, and the gap between p50 and p99 widens at every level. Three panels sharing one time axis say that more plainly than any single aggregate could, and the per-second resolution is what would expose a defect that the summary smooths away.
takeaways.base.conclusion: Two of those lines are judgement calls and are worth stating as such. **Stable throughput** is the best rung that still answered inside an acceptable tail - p95 under 500 ms with no errors - not the peak: at saturation throughput is at its highest and so is the queue behind it, so quoting the peak would describe a system nobody would choose to run. **Critical scenario** is the one that saturates at the lowest throughput rather than the one with the worst latency, because it is the first thing that breaks as real traffic grows.
takeaways.base.error_caveat: The error rate on the card counts the system's own failures: HTTP 5xx and dropped connections, which on this ladder are pool timeouts - the bottleneck named above. It deliberately excludes the routing 503s, because those are the measurement artifact proven under prediction #5: the fleet ages out mid-run while the agent simulator is stopped for determinism, and at 25 VUs that produced 175 of them. Counting a defect of the harness as a property of the system would put the wrong number in the specification.
